extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and readers of literary criticism (especially those interested in New Criticism and poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Cleanth Brooks's New Criticism principles for interpreting and teaching poetry, emphasizing close reading and the internal unity of the poem. Useful for critics, instructors, and students analyzing poetic form and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary concern: unity
rubrics_metrics.description: That the primary concern of criticism is with the problem of unity—the kind of whole which the literary work forms or fails to form, and the relation of the various parts to each other in building up this whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should focus on whether a work achieves an organic unity and how its parts contribute to that unity. Evaluate relations among elements (theme, imagery, structure) rather than treating passages in isolation. Anti-pattern: reading fragments without assessing their role within the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content inseparability
rubrics_metrics.description: That in a successful work, form and content cannot be separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how formal features (structure, meter, diction) shape and constitute meaning; do not analyze content divorced from its formal realization. Anti-pattern: treating plot/idea as independent of stylistic/formal choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form is meaning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take formal devices as central conveyors of meaning — rhythms, stanza form, repetition, and arrangement are not decorative but substantive. When scoring or judging, give weight to how form produces interpretive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature as metaphorical and symbolic
rubrics_metrics.description: That literature is ultimately metaphorical and symbolic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for figurative language and symbolic structures as primary sites of meaning; avoid literalizing poetic language. Examples: sustained metaphors, symbolic patterns that recur across the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal via the concrete
rubrics_metrics.description: That the general and the universal are not seized upon by abstraction, but got at through the concrete and the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive general or universal insights from close attention to particular images, incidents, and language in the poem rather than from abstract statements. Anti-pattern: making broad claims unsupported by specific textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature not a surrogate for religion / not didactic moralizer
rubrics_metrics.description: That literature is not a surrogate for religion. That, as Allen Tate says, 'specific moral problems' are the subject matter of literature, but that the purpose of literature is not to point a moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, distinguish a work's engagement with moral problems from an expectation that it deliver didactic moral lessons. Avoid judging a poem solely by its conformity to moral or religious doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles define area but not method
rubrics_metrics.description: That the principles of criticism define the area relevant to literary criticism; they do not constitute a method for carrying out the criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the articulated principles (unity, form-meaning, etc.) as guiding evaluative criteria but remain flexible in analytic techniques; the principles delimit concerns but do not prescribe a single procedural method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading of technical elements, patterns, and incongruities
rubrics_metrics.description: New Criticism involves examining a poem's 'technical elements, textual patterns, and incongruities' with a kind of scientific rigor and precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate attention to meter, rhyme, syntax, imagery, diction, repetitive patterns, and points of tension or contradiction. Good analysis documents these elements and explains how they contribute to the poem's effects and unity. Anti-pattern: vague impressions unbacked by textual detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism concerned primarily with the work itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The crux of New Criticism is that literary study be 'concerned primarily with the work itself' and 'by making the closest examination of what the poem says as a poem'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreground internal textual evidence; prioritize the poem's language, structure, and devices over external contexts when forming interpretations. Historical/biographical information may be used only insofar as it clarifies readings anchored in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Heresy of Paraphrase (resist reductionism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brooks's polemic against reducing a poem to a single narrative or didactic message—'The Heresy of Paraphrase'—argues poetry resists reduction through irony, paradox, ambiguity, and other rhetorical devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid summarizing a poem as its 'message'; instead analyze how conflicting facets, ambiguities, and tensions produce meaning. Anti-pattern: offering a neat paraphrase as the poem's definitive meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase, biography, and history as means not ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should resist reducing a poem to a simple paraphrase, explicating it through biographical or historical contexts, and interpreting it didactically; such background can be useful as a means to an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If biographical or historical information is introduced, show how it emerges from or is reflected in the poem's language and contributes to an internally grounded interpretation. Do not let context supplant close textual analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting the affective fallacy (avoid emotional-response evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brooks does not accept considering critics' emotional responses to works of literature as a legitimate approach to criticism; 'a detailed description of my emotional state...has little to do with indicating to an interested reader what the work is'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating criticism, prefer objective textual demonstration over reports of personal feeling as evidence. Anti-pattern: justifying interpretations primarily by 'how the poem made me feel.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of an ideal reader/central point of reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The formalist critic assumes an ideal reader: instead of focusing on the varying spectrum of possible readings, he attempts to find a central point of reference from which he can focus upon the structure of the poem or novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek an interpretive standpoint that makes sense of the poem's internal structure rather than treating all responses as equally authoritative. Be aware this is an assumption and justify the chosen reference point by textual analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach poetry as poetry (focus on language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brooks and Warren asserted poetry should be taught as poetry, and the critic should resist reducing a poem to biography, history, or morality; textbooks should emphasize the poem as language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pedagogy, center classroom work on close readings that illuminate how poetic language functions; use examples and exercises that isolate formal devices (meter, imagery, rhythm) and their interpretive consequences. Anti-pattern: teaching primarily via author biography or historical overview without textual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive context from language (internal contextual inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brooks maintained it is possible to derive a historical and biographical context from the language the poet uses; a poem 'does not depend for its success on outside knowledge that we bring to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When contextual interpretation is necessary, prefer explanations that show how language in the poem implies or constructs historical/biographical meanings, rather than importing outside facts that are disconnected from textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for paradox, irony, and tension as contributors to unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Brooks argued that irony, paradox, and opposing forces create tension and can produce a poem's unity rather than necessarily undermining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how contradictory elements are orchestrated to produce coherent aesthetic effects. Analyze how paradox and irony interact with other devices to create meaning and structural harmony. Anti-pattern: treating irony/paradox only as defects or incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to formal specifics: meter, rhyme, structure, imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fugitive group's close reading included considerations of a poem's form, structure, meter, rhyme scheme, and imagery; this formed the foundation for New Criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critical evaluation, list and interpret specific formal features (meter, rhyme, stanzaing, imagery) and explain their functional role within the poem's overall design. Avoid generalities; connect specifics to the poem's unity and meaning.
